Nice packaging is worth having once the parcel already survives the trip. A thank-you card inside a broken box buys nothing.

## One label, one parcel, the right item inside

Pack, check the label against the order, then seal. Two orders open on the same table at the same time is how the wrong item reaches the wrong person, and that mistake costs you two parcels, a refund and a review.

Then the habit that pays for itself the first time you need it: film the pack. One unbroken clip on your phone, from the open box with the item visible, through the filler and the tape, ending on the label with the order number readable. Ten seconds. Keep the clips until the orders close. When a buyer says the box was empty or the colour was wrong, that clip is the only thing that answers it.

## Handover and proof

Pickup or dropoff, choose the one that fits your week and repeat it on the same days. What matters is that no parcel leaves you without proof that it left: the courier's receipt, a scan against the tracking number, or a photo of the stack you handed over that day.

The tracking number is the parcel's identity. It belongs in your own record next to the order, not only inside an app.

## The five failures, and the move for each

**Stuck in transit.** Nothing scanned for days. Message the buyer before the buyer messages you, raise it with the courier through the channel your platform provides, and keep the reference of that report.

**Lost.** The same start, then a decision. When the courier's own process ends without the parcel, somebody absorbs it. Decide in advance whether you replace or refund, and then do it without being chased.

**Damaged on arrival.** Ask for photos of the item and the packaging together, before anything else. That pair tells you whether to change your packing or your courier, and any claim will need it.

**Wrong item sent.** This one is yours. Fix it quickly, apologise once, then go and look at your packing table.

**Returned to sender.** Nobody home, a wrong address, a refused COD parcel. It comes back and you have paid to move it twice. Note which buyer it was, because the same name coming back twice is information.

## Disputes and returns as an arrangement

Marketplace dispute processes share a shape. A buyer can raise a problem inside a window that opens at a certain stage of the order. Both sides put in evidence. The platform decides, and it decides on what is in the record.

The length of that window, who pays return shipping, what evidence counts, and how long a decision takes differ by platform and get changed. Do not carry them in your head, and do not take them from a seller group chat. Open the platform's current policy page while the case is open, and read the version that is live today.

Your job inside the process is boring: respond before the window closes, attach the packing clip and the handover proof, and write flat sentences with dates in them.

## A returns policy you can afford

Write your terms in the words a buyer will actually read, then check that you could pay for them in a bad week. A generous policy you quietly break is worse than a narrow one you keep.

Some fights cost more than the item. A replacement mug costs one mug. Three days of arguing costs three days, and the review lands anyway. Decide the peso line at which you stop arguing and simply replace, and decide it before you are angry.

When a review is unfair, keep the tone flat. One short public reply saying what happened and what you offered, then stop typing. That thread is being read by people deciding whether to buy from someone who behaves well when something goes wrong.

lessons.title: The week, and what to drop
lessons.content_mdx:
# The week, and what to drop

Aileen's week has no shape. Chats all day. Packing whenever there is a gap. Listings when there is energy left. Restocking after something has already run out.

That is not a busy shop. That is a shop with no week.

## Give every job a slot

The shop contains four jobs. Give each one a fixed place:

- **A photo and listing block.** One session, several products, one setup put up and taken down once.
- **A packing and handover window.** Tied to how your parcels leave, so packing finishes before they do.
- **Chat windows.** Two or three a day, at the hours you told buyers about, instead of all day at nobody's request.
- **A restock and numbers check.** One slot a week, the same day every week.

A slot is not a fantasy of a perfect week. It is what stops each job from depending on you remembering it at nine at night.

## Restock triggers instead of restock panics

Counting stock and reordering when it looks low is how a bestseller runs out in the middle of your busiest week.

Set a reorder point per product instead. It has two inputs and both are yours: how many you sell in a normal week, and how long your supplier or your own making takes to put stock back in your hands. Reorder when the count reaches what a normal week sells, multiplied by the weeks your supplier takes, plus a few units of slack. The slack is the point: a supplier who normally takes a week sometimes takes ten days, and some of your weeks will be busier than a normal one. Write it on the same sheet as your costs, so the weekly check is one look.

When you cannot restock in time, mark the listing out of stock. An out-of-stock listing costs you an order you were never going to fill. A cancelled order costs you the buyer, the refund handling, and whatever the platform counts against your shop.

## Which products actually pay you

Gut feel says your bestseller is your best product. Your cost sheet from chapter 3 and your payout statements say something else, and they are the ones holding evidence.

Once a month, put four things side by side for each product: units sold, pesos of margin per unit after every deduction, how many chats it generated, and how many came back. A product that sells steadily, earns little per unit, and produces the questions and the returns is a job you are paying to keep.

Dropping it is a decision, not a failure. Sell the remaining stock, take the listing down, and move the hours to the product that pays. Every hour in this shop is bought with something.

## Account health lives in your dashboard, not in the group chat

Marketplaces keep measures on sellers, in categories such as how you respond to buyers, how often you cancel, whether you dispatch on time, and how you are rated. They matter because they affect how your shop is treated.

What those measures are called, what counts as good, and what happens when you fall short all differ by platform and get changed. A number somebody posts in a seller group chat is a number from another platform, another category, or last year.

So treat it as a category you check yourself. Open your own seller dashboard on a fixed day, read what is shown for your shop today, and if something is flagged, fix the thing underneath it. Cancellations come from listing stock you do not have. Late dispatch comes from a packing window that is too small. Slow replies come from having no chat window and no standing replies.

## Spikes and holidays

A campaign or a Christmas rush multiplies the orders, not your hours.

- Pre-pack the bestsellers before the rush. Boxes taped, filler in, label added at the end.
- Cut the range you sell during the spike, so packing becomes repetitive instead of a puzzle.
- State the real dispatch window in the listing and in your chat note, then keep it. A wide honest window survives. A tight promise that slips becomes a cancellation, a complaint and a mark against the shop.
- Decide in advance which promotions you will join, using the floor price you set in chapter 3.

## When to add, when to get help, when to close

Three decisions come back every few months, and the same evidence answers all three.

Add a channel when the one you have keeps running out of hours, not when a new place is being talked about. Every new place is another inbox and another rulebook to keep up with.

Get help when one job has a fixed enough shape to hand over. Packing first, because it is the easiest to teach and the easiest to check.

Close a product line when the numbers have said so two months running and you are keeping it out of hope.

Then run the week again, and let the week carry the shop instead of you carrying it.

quiz.prompt: Aileen sells reed diffusers. A buyer messages: "Last price po? ₱250 na lang, bibili ako ng dalawa." Aileen's floor price for one unit, after every deduction, sits above ₱250. What is the reply that keeps the sale possible?

options.text: Accept ₱250 for the two units, since a repeat buyer who takes two is worth more than the margin on one order.
Ask what price the buyer had in mind, then settle between that and the listed price so the sale does not walk.
Offer the two-unit bundle she has costed, or the smaller size, and say her price once without repeating it.
Reply that the price is final and leave it there, since a buyer who opens with a haggle rarely buys anyway.

quiz.explanation: The floor price exists so this decision is already made: below it she is paying to work. What she still has are moves that are not discounts, and a bundle or a smaller variant answers too expensive without touching the floor. Asking what the buyer had in mind opens a negotiation with no bottom. A flat refusal with nothing offered throws away a sale she could have kept, and plenty of hagglers buy. Say the price once, because repeating it and explaining your costs reads as room to push.

quiz.prompt: Marisol's parcel to a buyer in Bacolod has not been scanned for six days. The buyer messages: "Ma'am wala pa rin po, scam ba to?" What is the best first reply?

options.text: Apologise, refund straight away, and file the report with the courier herself once the buyer has been made whole.
Send the tracking link and the courier hotline, so the buyer can chase the parcel while Marisol files her own report.
Ask the buyer to wait a few more days before either of them raises anything, since a stuck scan often clears on its own in the end.
Say what the tracking shows, that she is filing a report with the courier today, and when she will come back to the buyer.

quiz.explanation: An anxious buyer needs to know that a person has the problem and that something specific happens next. Facts she can see, an action with a date on it, and a promise to come back cover all three. Refunding first removes your leverage with the courier and trains the reflex for every future delay. Handing over a link and a hotline makes the buyer chase her own parcel, which is what she messaged to avoid. Asking for a few more days sets no date, files nothing, and leaves the buyer exactly where she was, only later.

quiz.prompt: A buyer leaves a one-star review saying the mug arrived cracked. Marisol's packing clip shows it left intact, and the buyer refused the replacement she offered. The review is public. What does she post?

options.text: One short reply that states what she offered and where a buyer can reach her, then nothing further on the thread.
A reply walking through the packing clip step by step, so that any reader can see the mug had left her table intact.
A reply asking the buyer to take the review down now that a replacement has been offered and then refused.
Nothing in public, and a private message repeating the offer, since replying only draws more eyes to the review.

quiz.explanation: The reply is written for the people reading the thread later, not for the reviewer. What they are judging is how this shop behaves when something goes wrong, and one calm line with an offer in it answers that. Arguing the clip point by point makes the shop look like the angry party even when the shop is right. Asking for a review to be taken down reads as pressure to every future reader and rarely works. Saying nothing in public leaves the buyer's version as the only version on the page, whatever she says privately.

quiz.prompt: Nico sells phone accessories from Marikina. He answers chats the second they arrive, all day, and his dispatch has started slipping because packing happens in whatever gap is left. What fixes the week?

options.text: Answer chats only after the day's parcels are packed, and let the morning messages wait until the evening.
Keep replying instantly and move packing to after the last pickup, since a fast answer is what turns a chat into an order.
Cut his range to the three products that generate the fewest questions, until dispatch has settled down again.
Set two chat windows a day, post those hours on the shop, and paste standing replies for the questions he answers daily.

quiz.explanation: Reply speed matters and so does dispatch, so the fix is not choosing between them but giving each one a slot. Published hours plus pasted answers hold a fast reply time without the phone owning the day. Making buyers wait until evening with no posted hours produces the follow-up messages he was trying to avoid, and packing after the last handover means the parcels miss it. Cutting the range is a real decision he may make later on evidence from his own numbers, but here it gives up products to fix a week that simply has no shape.

quiz.prompt: A buyer opens a case saying the box held a black case, not the blue one she ordered. Nico is sure he packed blue, but he has no record of that order beyond the waybill number. What should he do now, and change from today?

options.text: Hold firm and reply that he packed the order himself and remembers the blue case going into that box.
Send the replacement now, and from today film one unbroken clip per parcel, ending on a label the camera can read.
Ask the buyer to send the black case back to him first, then decide whether the claim was honest before he replaces it.
Refund in full and stop stocking colour variants, since a colour claim is the one thing he can never prove.

quiz.explanation: With no evidence this case is already lost, so pay the cheap version of it and buy the habit that stops the next one. A ten second clip that runs from the open box to a label you can actually read is the only thing that answers an empty-box or wrong-item claim later, and a clip that ends on a blurred label answers nothing. Remembering is not evidence and reads as an argument. Demanding the item back first is reasonable once you have proof, but here it stalls a buyer he cannot contradict. Dropping variants throws away sales to fix a record-keeping problem.

quiz.prompt: Aileen's bestselling scent ran out in the middle of her busiest week and she cancelled four orders. Her supplier needs about a week to refill her. What stops this happening again?

options.text: Order double of everything at the next restock, so that she is never caught short on any product again.
Keep the listing up during the gap and tell each buyer there is a short wait while the stock is refilled.
Set a reorder point covering a week of normal sales plus slack, and check it in her weekly numbers slot.
Check the stock count every morning and reorder the moment a product looks low on the shelf.

quiz.explanation: A reorder point turns restocking into arithmetic instead of memory, and both inputs are hers: what a normal week sells, and how long the supplier takes. The slack is the part people drop. Set it to exactly one week of normal sales and every busier-than-normal week is a stockout, and a supplier who normally takes a week sometimes takes ten days. Buying double across the range ties up cash in the products that do not move and does nothing for the one that does. Selling what she cannot dispatch converts an out-of-stock listing, which costs her an order, into cancellations, which cost her the buyers. A daily eyeball is the same guess run more often.

quiz.prompt: Nico opens his own seller dashboard and reads the measures shown for his shop today. Cancellations are flagged. Both of this month's cancellations happened after he listed stock he did not actually have. What should he do about the flag?

options.text: Fix the habit underneath it: one stock count, changed the moment a parcel leaves, so he stops selling what is gone.
Hold himself to two cancellations a month, which is the line a seller group says the platform draws for a shop like his.
Ask the next buyer who has to be cancelled on to cancel from their side, so it is not recorded against his shop.
Dispatch the doubtful orders late rather than cancel them, since a late parcel annoys a buyer less than a cancellation.

quiz.explanation: The dashboard tells him what is being measured on his shop now, which is the only version that counts, and a line remembered from a group chat is another platform's line or last year's. Once he has read it, the flag is not the problem: the cause is. Both cancellations came from listing stock he did not have, so one count changed the moment a parcel leaves is what removes them. Capping cancellations by willpower does not stop the next oversell. Pushing the cancellation onto the buyer asks a stranger to cover for him and may be recorded anyway, and swapping cancellations for late dispatch moves the mark to another measure.

quiz.prompt: A month later a different buyer files a return request saying her mug arrived cracked. Marisol has read the platform's current policy page and she is inside the window to respond. What does she ask the buyer for, and what does she attach herself?

options.text: A photo of the crack on its own, attached with her courier receipt for the day that parcel was handed over.
A video of the buyer opening the parcel, attached with the supplier's photo of the mug as it left the factory.
The waybill number and the buyer's own account of what happened, attached with her written packing routine.
A photo of the mug and its packaging together, attached with her packing clip ending on the readable label.

quiz.explanation: The pair is the point. A crack photographed on its own says the mug is broken and nothing about how. The mug lying in its own filler and mailer shows whether the packing failed or the parcel was crushed, which tells her whether to change her packing or her courier, and any claim will need it. Her own clip, running unbroken from the open box to a label the camera can read, is the other half: it shows what left her table. An unboxing video is the buyer's to make or refuse, a factory photo is somebody else's promise, and a written routine describes every parcel rather than this one.

assignment.title: One Product, From Listing to Payout
assignment.brief_mdx:
Pick one product you could actually sell this month. Your own stock, something you make, or something you resell for someone else. It has to be real enough that you can hold it, photograph it and find out what it costs you. Everything below is about that one product and the shop you would run around it.

Submit one text document with seven parts. No images and no uploads. Where photos are asked for, describe them in words.

1. **The product decision.** What the product is, and how you get stock: bought and held by you, made to order, or held by a supplier or consignor. Then the handling reality in a few lines: size, weight, fragility, shelf life if it has one, whether it needs sizes or colours, and what one damaged unit costs you to replace. Finish with the demand you have seen with your own eyes. What people already ask you for, what already sells near you, what you could restock next week. Not a trend somebody told you about.

2. **The channel.** Name the one or two selling places you would actually start in. For each one, write what it gives you and what it takes back. Then name a place you are not using and say why not.

3. **The listing, written out ready to paste.**
   - A title built from the words a buyer would type, local and Taglish terms included.
   - An ordered shot list. For each shot: what is in the frame, and the buyer question it answers. One of them has to show scale. One of them has to show condition, including any flaw.
   - The full description, in the order a buyer decides: what they receive, the details that decide fit, condition, how it is packed and dispatched, and your terms.
   - Your variations as real options with stock against each, not a line telling people to message you for other colours.

4. **The cost and price sheet, in pesos, per unit.** Item cost, cost of getting it to you, packaging and filler, the label, any freebie you include, and a share for breakage and for stock that never sells. Put a peso value on your own hours and say how you arrived at it. Then list the deduction categories that come out of a payout on your chosen channel, one line each, and fill in the current figure from that platform's published rate card. **Beside every fee, rate, charge or courier price you write, name where you found it and the date you looked.** If a figure is not published, or you could not confirm it, write the line item anyway and say so instead of guessing. Nobody is checking whether your figure is right. They are checking that you can say where it came from and when. Close with your list price, your floor price, and one promotion or campaign you would refuse because it would price you under that floor.

5. **Shipping and returns, in the words a buyer will read.** Who pays for delivery, whether you accept cash on delivery, your dispatch window, what happens when an item arrives damaged or wrong, and what you will not take back. Write it as the buyer sees it. Then add one line addressed to your reviewer: how you can afford these terms at the floor price you just set.

6. **Five standing replies.** Written the way you would send them. Include a buyer asking for a discount, a buyer asking where their order is, and a buyer whose parcel went back to sender. Choose the other two from the questions you expect daily. Keep them short, specific and boring, because anything you type can end up in a dispute or a screenshot.

7. **The week.** Your fixed slots for photos and listings, packing and handover, chats, and a restock check, each with a day and a rough number of hours. State how many hours a week you actually have. Add one restock trigger: the stock level that makes you reorder, and how you would notice you had hit it.

Before you submit, do one check. Read your five replies, then read your listing. Every question those replies answer should already be answered in the listing. If it is not, edit the listing. Answering the same question twice a day forever is the thing this assignment exists to save you from.
criteria: The product decision names how stock is obtained, the physical handling reality including what one damaged unit costs to replace, and demand the learner has personally seen rather than an assumed trend; the channel section names one or two specific selling places and states, for each, what it gives the seller and what it takes back

The listing is complete and pasteable: a title in the words a buyer would type, a description covering what is received, the details that decide fit, condition and terms, and variations carrying their own stock rather than an instruction to message for other options
The shot list is ordered, every shot states the buyer question it answers, and it includes a shot that shows scale and a shot that shows condition, not only a hero shot and close-ups

The cost sheet arithmetic is correct when the reviewer adds it up, and it carries packaging, a share for breakage or unsold stock, and a peso value on the learner's own hours with a stated basis; a list price, a floor price and one refused promotion are named, and the refused promotion would genuinely breach that floor

Every fee, rate, charge or courier price in the submission is followed by where the learner looked it up and the date they looked, or by a plain statement that it could not be confirmed. The reviewer checks that a source and a date are named, not that the figure is correct, and returns any submission that asserts a percentage, a rate or a threshold with neither

The shipping and returns terms are written for a buyer to read and are affordable at the stated floor price, the five replies cover a discount request, a where-is-my-order and a return to sender, and the weekly routine has fixed slots plus a restock trigger that fit inside the hours the learner says they have
